ap_chemistry-m01.stem: The first ionization energy of aluminum (578 kJ/mol) is lower than that of magnesium (738 kJ/mol), even though aluminum has the larger nuclear charge. Which statement best explains this observation?

options.text: Aluminum atoms are larger than magnesium atoms because they have more electron shells.
options.why: Both atoms have three shells, so the shell count does not explain the lower ionization energy of Al.

options.text: The outermost electron of Al is in a 3p subshell, which is higher in energy and farther from the nucleus than the 3s subshell of Mg, so it is easier to remove.
options.why: A 3p electron is held less tightly than a 3s electron because it is less penetrating, which outweighs the added proton.

options.text: The outermost electron of Al is paired in a 3s orbital, so repulsion removes it more easily.
options.why: The outermost electron of Al is a single 3p electron, not a paired 3s electron.

options.text: Aluminum has fewer protons than magnesium, so its nucleus attracts electrons less strongly.
options.why: Aluminum has 13 protons and magnesium has 12, so the nuclear charge is larger for aluminum.

facts: The first ionization energy of aluminum (578 kJ/mol) is lowe

options.text: Sulfur atoms have a smaller radius than phosphorus atoms, so the outer electrons are held more weakly.
options.why: A smaller radius generally raises, not lowers, the ionization energy.

options.text: A 3p orbital of sulfur holds a pair of electrons, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove than an unpaired electron of phosphorus.
options.why: Electron–electron repulsion in a doubly occupied 3p orbital lowers the energy needed to remove an electron.

options.text: The outermost electron of sulfur is in a 4s subshell, which is farther from the nucleus.
options.why: The outermost electrons of sulfur are in the 3p subshell, as in phosphorus.

ap_chemistry-m02.stem: A student needs 250.0 mL of a 0.100 M NaCl solution from solid NaCl. Which procedure is most appropriate for making the solution accurately?

options.text: Add 1.461 g of NaCl to a 250.0 mL graduated cylinder, then add 250.0 mL of water and stir until it dissolves.
options.why: Adding 250.0 mL of water to the solid makes more than 250.0 mL of solution, so the concentration is too low.

options.text: Dissolve 1.461 g of NaCl in water in a beaker, transfer it to a 250.0 mL volumetric flask with rinsings, and fill to the mark.
options.why: Dissolving first, transferring completely, and filling to the calibration mark gives exactly 250.0 mL of solution with the intended amount of solute.

options.text: Dissolve 14.61 g of NaCl in water and dilute the solution to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask.
options.why: Using 14.61 g gives a concentration ten times too large.

options.text: Add 1.461 g of NaCl to a beaker and fill the beaker with water until it reaches the 250 mL line on its side.
options.why: A beaker's markings are not accurate enough to prepare a solution of a precise concentration.

ap_chemistry-m02.stem: A student has 1.00 M HCl and needs 100.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl. Which procedure is most appropriate for the dilution?

options.text: Pour 100.0 mL of the 1.00 M HCl into a beaker that holds 10.00 mL of water and stir the mixture.
options.why: This produces a solution that is far more concentrated than 0.100 M.

options.text: Pour 10.00 mL of the 1.00 M HCl into a beaker that holds 100.0 mL of water and stir the mixture.
options.why: This makes about 110 mL of solution, so the concentration is below 0.100 M, and the volumes are not measured accurately.

options.text: Pipet 10.00 mL of the 1.00 M HCl into a 100.0 mL volumetric flask that holds some water, then add water to the mark.
options.why: The moles of HCl in 10.00 mL of 1.00 M acid are 0.0100 mol, which gives 0.100 M in 100.0 mL, and a pipet and flask measure the volumes accurately.

options.text: Pipet 1.00 mL of the 1.00 M HCl into a 100.0 mL volumetric flask and add water to the mark.
options.why: This makes 0.0100 M HCl, which is ten times too dilute.

facts: A student has 1.00 M HCl and needs 100.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl.

ap_chemistry-m03.stem: Chlorine gas is bubbled through a colorless solution of sodium bromide, and the solution turns orange as Br₂ forms. Which particle-level statement best describes the change?

options.text: Br⁻ ions gain electrons to form Br₂ molecules, and Cl₂ molecules lose electrons to form Cl⁻ ions.
options.why: Forming Br₂ from Br⁻ requires a loss of electrons, so it is oxidation.

options.text: Cl₂ molecules gain electrons to form Cl⁻ ions, and Br⁻ ions lose electrons to form Br₂ molecules.
options.why: Chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidized, so electrons transfer from Br⁻ to Cl₂.

options.text: Cl₂ molecules and Br⁻ ions share electrons to form BrCl molecules.
options.why: The orange color is from Br₂, and the change is an electron transfer rather than sharing to form BrCl.

options.text: Na⁺ ions gain electrons from Cl₂ and form sodium atoms.
options.why: Sodium ions are spectators here and are not reduced.

facts: Chlorine gas is bubbled through a colorless solution of sodi
